To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
income inequality at the commune level is associated with HIV burden among persons who inject drugs in Thai Nguyen province.
income inequality in the community is associated with higher HIV prevalence in persons who inject drugs in Thai Nguyen, and that this association is not explained by income at the individual level.
income inequality at the neighborhood level is associated with HIV infection among PWID in Vietnam.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between income inequality, income, and HIV in the context of a concentrated epidemic.
the relationship between income inequality, socioeconomic factors and HIV prevalence.
the association between community level income inequality and individual level HIV infection among persons who inject drugs in a concentrated HIV epidemic setting in Vietnam.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the association between income and HIV is complex and that both income inequality and absolute level of income are important factors to consider in the epidemiological and social context of HIV.
income inequality is associated at the community level with HIV infection in PWIDs in a concentrated epidemic, and that this association is independent of individual income.
community level income inequality is associated, in a non linear fashion, with HIV prevalence among persons who inject drugs in a concentrated epidemic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the higher the income inequality, the higher the HIV burden in PWID.
income inequality is a better predictor of HIV prevalence in a concentrated epidemic, and that income inequality and individual income should be considered together as determinants of HIV prevalence.
income inequality at the local level is associated with HIV risk in PWID in Vietnam, even after controlling for individual level income and other community level variables.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the association between income and HIV is not straightforward, but that income inequality is a more powerful predictor of HIV prevalence than absolute income.
the community level GINI coefficient is a better predictor of HIV prevalence than the individual level GINI coefficient or the absolute median income.

the community level socioeconomic context is an important factor to be considered in designing interventions to reduce HIV burden in a concentrated epidemic, and that interventions that target individual socioeconomic status may have limited impact if the broader community level context is not taken into account.
